text:
It was Monsieur Lheureux, the merchant, who had taken charge of the order;
this gave him the opportunity to visit Emma. He talked with her
about the new goods being unpacked in Paris, about a thousand feminine curiosities, showed
himself very obliging, and never asked for money. Emma
gave herself over to this ease of satisfying all her whims. Thus,
she wanted to have, in order to give it to Rodolphe, a very fine riding crop
that was in an umbrella shop in Rouen. The following week,
Monsieur Lheureux set it down on her table.

But the next day he called at her house with a bill for two
hundred and seventy francs, not counting the centimes. Emma was greatly
embarrassed: all the drawers of the writing desk were empty; more than
a fortnight’s wages were owed to Lestiboudois, two quarters’ wages to the maid,
and a great many other things besides, and Bovary was impatiently awaiting
the remittance from Monsieur Derozerays, who was accustomed to pay him
every year around Saint Peter’s Day.

At first she managed to send Lheureux away; at last he lost patience; his
creditors were after him, his capital was tied up, and if some of it did not
come in, he would be forced to take back from her all the goods
she had.

“Why, take them back!” said Emma.

“Oh! You’re joking!” he replied. “The only thing I regret is the
riding crop. Upon my word! I shall ask Monsieur for it back.”

“No! No!” she said.

“Ah! I’ve got you!” Lheureux thought.

And, sure of what he had discovered, he went out, repeating under his breath
and with his usual little whistle:

“Very well! We shall see! We shall see!”

She was wondering how to get herself out of this when the cook came in and
placed on the mantelpiece a small roll of blue paper, sent by Monsieur
Derozerays. Emma pounced on it and opened it. There were fifteen napoleons.
It was the payment. She heard Charles on the stairs; she threw
the gold into the back of her drawer and took the key.

Three days later, Lheureux reappeared.

“I have an arrangement to propose to you,” he said; “if, instead of the sum
agreed upon, you would be willing to take...”

“Here it is,” she said, placing fourteen napoleons in his hand.

The merchant was astounded. Then, to conceal his disappointment,
he launched into apologies and offers of service, all of which Emma refused;
then she remained for a few minutes fingering in the pocket of her
apron the two five-franc coins he had given her in change. She promised
herself she would economize, so as to pay them back later...

“Bah!” she thought. “He will not think of it again.”

Besides the riding crop with its gilt-silver knob, Rodolphe had received a seal
with this motto: _Love in the heart_; in addition, a scarf to make himself
a muffler, and lastly a cigar case exactly like the Viscount’s,
which Charles had once picked up on the road and which Emma had kept.
Yet these gifts humiliated him. He refused several of them; she
insisted, and Rodolphe finally obeyed, finding her tyrannical and too
encroaching.

Then she had strange ideas:

“When midnight strikes,” she would say, “you will think of me!”

And if he admitted that he had not thought of her, there would be reproaches
galore, always ending with the eternal phrase:

“Do you love me?”

“Why yes, I love you!” he would answer.

“A lot?”

“Certainly!”

“You haven’t loved others, have you?”

“Do you think you took me as a virgin?” he would exclaim, laughing.

Emma would weep, and he would try to console her, embellishing his
protestations with puns.

“Oh! It is because I love you!” she would resume. “I love you so much that I
cannot do without you, do you understand? Sometimes I have such longings to
see you again that all the rages of love tear me apart. I ask myself: ‘Where
is he? Perhaps he is talking to other women? They smile at him, he draws
closer...’ Oh! No, isn’t that so, none of them pleases you? There are women
more beautiful; but I know how to love better! I am your servant and
your concubine! You are my king, my idol! You are good! You are handsome! You
are intelligent! You are strong!”

He had heard these things said to him so many times that they held
nothing original for him. Emma resembled all mistresses;
and the charm of novelty, gradually falling away like a garment,
laid bare the eternal monotony of passion, which always has
the same forms and the same language. This man, so full of experience,
did not distinguish the dissimilarity of feelings beneath the sameness of
expressions. Because wanton or venal lips had
murmured similar phrases to him, he had little faith in the
sincerity of hers; one had to make allowances, he thought, exaggerated words
concealing mediocre affections; as though the fullness of the soul did not
sometimes overflow through the emptiest metaphors,
since no one can ever give the exact measure of his
needs, or his conceptions, or his sorrows, and human speech
is like a cracked cauldron on which we beat out tunes to make
bears dance when we would like to move the stars to pity.

But, with that superiority of judgment belonging to one who,
in any involvement whatsoever, holds himself back, Rodolphe perceived
in this love other pleasures to exploit. He deemed all modesty
inconvenient. He treated her without ceremony. He made of her something
pliant and corrupt. It was a kind of idiotic attachment full
of admiration for him, of sensual pleasures for her, a bliss that
benumbed her; and her soul sank into that intoxication and drowned there,
shriveling like the Duke of Clarence in his butt of malmsey.

Through the effect of her amorous habits alone, Madame Bovary changed
her demeanor. Her glances became bolder, her speech freer;
she even had the impropriety to walk about with Monsieur Rodolphe, a
cigarette in her mouth, as though to thumb her nose at the world; finally,
those who still doubted doubted no longer when, one day, she was seen getting
down from the Hirondelle, her waist confined in a waistcoat, in the manner of
a man; and Madame Bovary the elder, who, after a dreadful scene with her
husband, had come to take refuge with her son, was not the least scandalized
of the respectable ladies. Many other things displeased her: first, Charles
had not heeded her advice about banning novels; then,
the way the household was run displeased her; she allowed herself to make
remarks, and they quarreled, especially once, over Félicité.

The previous evening, as Madame Bovary the elder was crossing the corridor,
she had caught her in the company of a man, a man with a brown collar,
about forty years old, who, at the sound of her footsteps, had
quickly slipped out of the kitchen. Then Emma began to laugh; but the good
lady flew into a rage, declaring that unless one meant to make a mockery of
morals, one had to keep watch over those of the servants.
